correctness.rationale: Deleting one entry from a decreasing layer decrements its length or drops a singleton, without merging other layers. Terminal-one encoding sends a decrement to deletion of a zero, and a singleton removal to deletion of a 1 from the initial run or from a run of length at least two; deleting any equivalent 1 in that run yields the same output. Independently reconstructed the ordinary binary lemma: if L,R are first/last differences, any common output using deletions at i≤j in the two words can be represented by deletions at L,R, since the positions from i to L in the first and from R to j in the second lie in constant runs by the intervening shift equality. The opposite alignment gives the only other possible output; if L=R there is just one. For L<R two distinct outputs occur precisely when both shift equalities hold through the differing interval, forcing opposite alternating phases over a binary alphabet. The resulting endpoint-zero deletions are always allowed. The other output uses the first and last endpoint ones; the first is deletable only at the beginning or just after a common 1, and the last only just before a common 1 (with equivalent deletion elsewhere in its run allowed). The final 1 lies in the common suffix. Reading the two parities, including the shared following 1, gives exactly the two moves with t≥1 and unique boundaries. Counting marked blocks yields ((1−z)/(1−2z))² z³/(1−z). Heavy parts and gap weights and two-presence are preserved; swaps let two 1s flank a 2, then 121→22 reduces their count to the parity normal form, proving sufficiency and the Fibonacci size product. The gap series for components and isolated vertices are respectively (1+z²)/(1−z) and 1/(1−z)+z², separated by heavy parts of series z³/(1−z), giving both stated rational functions and the n=0 convention. Independent reverse-deck indexing and union-find in /workspace/reviews/evidence/layered_replay.py exhaust n=1 through 11: all edges match their proposed moves uniquely, no pair shares more than two outputs, and all component signatures, sizes and counts agree, including (1280,396,288) at n=11. This is corroboration, not the all-n proof. Frozen scripts were inspected rather than executed.
residual_risks: No claim concerning full permutation classes, maximum independent sets, or k-deletion decks.
Independent enumeration is finite; the alignment and canonical-form arguments establish the infinite claims.

evidence: Vatter proves reconstruction from the full set of k-deletions for n≥3k+1, sharp at 3k. Raykova analyzes layered full-set reconstruction thresholds (including L′_k>k+log₂ k). A full deck can distinguish vertices that still share two individual minor types.

Cai et al. give the general Type-A alternating criterion; Resultary 737fed325e91 counts unrestricted word edges, and bd47d6c96416 describes a complete fiber of a particular composition k-deletion set. None directly counts the admissible edges or same-rank components of the frozen graph.
broader_coverage.reasoning: The unrestricted theorem is essential prior local machinery, but deletion filtering and component connectivity require separate arguments. Deck reconstruction and deck fibers solve different inference questions.
searches: Resultary unrestricted q-ary two-read (737fed325e91) and critical composition deck fibers (bd47d6c96416)

evidence: An induced subgraph merely restricting vertices to words ending in 1 would still count the pair 0011 and 0101. They have ordinary common outputs 011 and 001; 001 requires deleting an inadmissible isolated 1 from 0101, so the compositions (3,1) and (2,2) have only one common permitted minor. Thus vertex restriction alone cannot specialize the unrestricted edge theorem to this graph.

The component proof uses swapping the 1 past a 2 and consolidating 121↔22, and excludes the all-singleton gap. Adjacent-position swap components and the two-read graph for words avoiding 11 are not computations for this move system.
claim_vs_prior_implication.reasoning: The filter matters even for concrete low-order pairs, and the all-length component/canonical-form, gap independence and enumerations are not automatic consequences of the unrestricted formulas or of OEIS.

evidence: McNamara–Sagan identify layered-permutation order with generalized subword order on compositions; the graph compares same-rank pairs by shared lower covers, not the topology or Möbius function of a single interval.

Resultary 920b1e1645a1 is the same vertex language with adjacent-position swaps and Fibonacci-cube components. Its (1,1)–(2) edge at n=2 is absent here since both vertices have only one minor; conversely (1,2)–(2,1) at n=3 joins 132 and 213, which are not related by one adjacent swap.

originality.rationale: The ordinary alternating-interval criterion, composition deletion channel, and edge-number sequence are prior and must remain credited. The claim that survives comparison is the restricted graph's admissibility-filtered moves, which yield new exact ambiguity-component signatures, Fibonacci product sizes, and enumerators for this adjacency. Same-day results on similar graphs or on the same source under different adjacency do not supply this classification.

checked_sources: Frozen RESULT.md, component and enumeration statements
Vatter and Cai et al. problem frameworks
value.rationale: The layered source comes from an established reconstruction problem. A local ambiguity rule propagates into a global classification over an exponentially large source, with exact decomposition and independently useful enumeration of component sizes and singleton behavior. This is more than another interpretation of a known edge sequence. It tells a coding researcher which families of vertices must be considered together, without assuming that a component's code capacity is determined by its size.
residual_risks: The result does not solve the independent-set/codebook problems within the nontrivial components.
